title: Grand County Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Grand County wells have a 190-foot median depth and 9 gpm median yield. Review local drilling costs, water levels and checks before buying land.
h1: What to Expect From a Well in Grand County
intro_html:
A Grand County well is usually a mountain-bedrock job, and the water depends on the fractures the drill reaches. County records show a median depth of 190 feet and a median reported yield of 9 gpm, but neither is a promise for an individual lot.

Colorado DWR records contain 11,182 permits in the county, with 6,871 wells recorded as constructed. For property around Granby, Fraser, Grand Lake or Kremmling, use those records to find nearby completed wells—not just nearby permit locations—before setting a budget.

sections.heading: Budget for Bedrock, Not Just Grand County’s Median Depth
sections.html:
The 7,350 wells reporting depth have a median of 190 feet, with the middle half between 100 and 325 feet. That spread matters when comparing bids: a quote based only on the median leaves considerable room for additional drilling. The 90th-percentile depth is 500 feet, so deeper work is part of the local picture.

Permits classify 11,013 wells as unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer wells, compared with 46 labeled Alluvial and 28 labeled Troublesome. In granite and gneiss, usable water comes from connected fractures rather than a dependable underground layer. Around Tabernash or Hot Sulphur Springs, nearby completion logs are a better starting point than assuming the county median fits your parcel.

sections.heading: A Reported 9 gpm Is Useful, but Test the Actual Well
sections.html:
Among 3,445 wells with reported pump yields, the median is 9 gpm and the middle half runs from 6 to 11.5 gpm. Most reported results fall in the 5–15 gpm group, which accounts for 74%. Those figures are encouraging for household supply, but a completion-record yield does not establish dependable output under every operating condition.

The low end deserves attention: 14% report 1–5 gpm, and 1% report under 1 gpm. A low-producing well can require storage and careful demand management. Before buying, have sustained pumping and recovery evaluated. A larger pump cannot make the surrounding fractures deliver more water, and recorded yield does not establish permission for irrigation or other uses.

sections.heading: Grand County Water Levels Do Not Show a Steady Recent Drop
sections.html:
Static water level is where water stands in a resting well, not the bottom of the drilled hole. Among 932 reported measurements, the median is 80 feet below ground, with the middle half between 37 and 100 feet. Pump selection also needs the water level during pumping, not just this resting measurement.

Decade medians deepen from 35 feet in the 1970s to 60 in the 1980s and 90 in the 1990s. They then sit at 80 feet in the 2000s, 2010s and 2020s. That does not show a continuing recent countywide decline. These are measurements from different wells, however, not repeated readings from a fixed monitoring network; they cannot establish the trend at your property.

sections.heading: Grand County’s Busiest Permit Years and Recorded Drillers
sections.html:
The largest decade totals were 2,618 permits in the 1990s and 2,337 in the 2000s. Records show 970 in the 2010s and 908 in the 2020s, with the newest permit dated 2026. The current decade is incomplete, so its total is not a full-decade comparison. Permit issuance also does not mean every authorized well was built.

Mcpherson Drilling Company (Mcpherson, Benny Don) appears in 1,840 records, James Drilling (Keaton, Jordan K.) in 720, and Virginia Drilling Co. Inc. (Shuck, Otis C) in 447. These are historical record counts, not confirmation of current availability. Domestic/household use accounts for 86% of the use mix, making residential supply the dominant recorded purpose.

sections.heading: A New Grand County Well: Hole Price Versus Finished Supply
sections.html:
The local drilling model uses $65–$100 per foot for fractured mountain bedrock. At the 190-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole at about $12,400–$19,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at $18,400–$31,000. Treat these as budgeting ranges, not parcel-specific quotes.

The 100–325-foot middle depth range explains why a single fixed allowance can miss the mark. Ask bidders how extra footage, casing and grout are charged, and what happens if the hole produces poorly. Around Winter Park or Grand Lake, have the contractor review rig access and the route to the house before pricing. Make sure every bid separates drilling from the equipment and site work needed to deliver water indoors.

sections.heading: Check Grand County Water Quality and Site Constraints Together
sections.html:
The supplied environmental inventory lists 10 PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 85 historic mine features and 5 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Those mapped features are reasons to investigate proximity and groundwater pathways, not proof that a particular well is contaminated. A PFAS sampling location is not automatically a confirmed contamination source.

For an existing well, obtain a laboratory water test and discuss location-specific testing with the lab or local health authority. Inspect the wellhead, casing and surface drainage. For a new lot, fractured rock carries low-yield and dry-hole risk even near successful wells. Lay out the septic system, replacement area, building footprint and drilling access together so the well location meets applicable setbacks and remains accessible for service.

sections.heading: Before Closing on Land in Fraser, Parshall or Kremmling
sections.html:
Start with the parcel’s actual DWR permit and any construction, pump-installation and testing records. Confirm that the permitted uses match your plans. A household-use permit should not be assumed to cover lawn watering, livestock or another dwelling; additional uses may need different authorization or an augmentation plan, depending on the water-rights setting.

Next, compare completed wells on similar nearby terrain in Fraser, Parshall or Kremmling rather than relying on countywide averages. For an existing supply, make water quality and pumping performance part of due diligence. For vacant land, get a driller’s site review and coordinate driveway, septic and home placement before committing to a building layout. Keep deeper drilling and poor production in the financial discussion.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Grand County, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth in Grand County is 190 feet. The middle half falls between 100 and 325 feet, and the 90th-percentile depth is 500 feet. Fractured mountain bedrock makes depth unpredictable from lot to lot, so review nearby completed-well logs before accepting a drilling allowance based on the median.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Grand County?
faq.a: The Grand County cost model uses $65–$100 per foot. At the median depth of 190 feet, the drilled hole is about $12,400–$19,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $18,400–$31,000. Ask for a site-specific bid that explains extra footage, casing, access and poorly producing holes.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Grand County?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a median of 9 gpm, with the middle half between 6 and 11.5 gpm. Under 1 gpm accounts for 1% of reported yields, while 14% fall between 1 and 5 gpm. Before buying, test the actual well’s pumping performance and recovery rather than treating its historical yield as guaranteed output.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Grand County?
faq.a: County permit records cannot establish drinking-water safety for an individual well. The mapped environmental inventory includes 10 PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 85 historic mine features and 5 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites within about 10 miles. These warrant location-specific review, not a blanket contamination finding. Obtain laboratory testing and inspect the wellhead before relying on the supply.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Grand County?
faq.a: The supplied measurements do not show a steady recent countywide decline. Median static water depth was 90 feet in the 1990s and 80 feet in the 2000s, 2010s and 2020s. These decade groups contain different wells, so they cannot establish a parcel-level trend. Review the property’s own measurement and pumping history where available.
